text: Mars was a Continental Celtic and British god. When the Roman legions subjugated Celtic tribal lands, they practiced the interpretatio romana, calling local divinities by Roman names. Thus we have more than 60 versions of Mars, the Roman god of agriculture who, in later times, became a god of war. Whether the Celts saw their own Mars as connecting war and agriculture is not evident. Some inscriptions and sculptures suggest as much, especially those that depict Mars in warrior's attire holding a cornucopia filled with the fruits of the harvest. Mars is in some cases described as a protector of the people, identified with the god Teutates, ruler of the people. Other commentators suggest that the Celtic Mars may have been a god of the wildwood or of healing. Typical depictions of Mars show him in Celtic military garb, sometimes wearing a twisted-metal torc. In some cases Mars is shown naked, carrying a weapon, a reference to the tradition of Celtic warriors going to war without clothing. Another Celtic motif appears in the occasional multiplication of Mars into three gods. Mars figures are especially found in Britain and, on the Continent, among the Belgai and the Remi. These surnames appear: Mars Alator, Albiorix, world-king of the Albici, Beatucadrus, Caturix, battle-king, Lenus, a healing spring god of Trier, Lucetius, and Rigisamus, king of kings.
objective: Document Mars, the Continental Celtic and British god renamed by the interpretatio romana.
